back: High sampling rate, no reaction time, long unattended recording, direct transfer to computer.
Readings taken per second — must be high enough to capture the event.
To model systems too big, small, fast, slow, dangerous or costly to test — then check against data.
A device that automatically records readings from one or more sensors at set time intervals, for later analysis on a computer.

front: A collision lasting 20 ms is logged at 10 samples per second. Problem?
back: The interval between samples (0.1 s) is longer than the event, so it may be missed entirely. The sampling rate must be high enough to give many points during the event.

front: Match sensors to quantities: motion sensor, light gate, force sensor, temperature probe.
back: Motion sensor: position/velocity (ultrasound echo). Light gate: time of interruption → speed. Force sensor: force (e.g. in collisions). Temperature probe: thermistor-based temperature.

front: How does an ultrasonic motion sensor measure distance?
back: It emits ultrasound pulses and times the echo: distance $= \dfrac{v_{\text{sound}} \times t}{2}$ (there and back). Repeated pulses give velocity and acceleration.

front: Disadvantages or limitations of data loggers?
back: Cost; sensors need calibration; a sensor’s own resolution and response time limit the data; errors can go unnoticed if the output is not checked.

front: Why and how is a sensor calibrated?
back: To make its output match true values: record its readings at known reference values (e.g. ice point and boiling water for a temperature probe) and correct accordingly.

front: How can video analysis measure motion, and what limits it?
back: Record the motion beside a scale, then step frame by frame: displacement from the scale, time from the frame rate. A low frame rate limits time resolution and causes motion blur.

front: Why use a spreadsheet for processing data?
back: It repeats calculations (means, uncertainties, derived quantities) quickly and without arithmetic slips, plots graphs and fits trend lines, and updates everything if a value changes.

front: How does a spreadsheet model the motion of a falling object with drag?
back: Step through small time intervals Δt: find $a$ from the forces at the current $v$, then $v_{\text{new}} = v + a\Delta t$ and $s_{\text{new}} = s + v\Delta t$, and repeat.

front: In an iterative model, what is the effect of making the time step Δt smaller?
back: The model becomes more accurate (it assumes quantities are constant for a shorter time), at the cost of more calculation steps.

front: Can a simulation’s output be trusted on its own?
back: No. It is only as good as its assumptions and inputs; its predictions must be checked against real experimental data.

front: What are the limitations of a computer model?
back: It simplifies reality (e.g. ignores drag, assumes ideal behaviour), so results are only valid within its assumptions and the range tested.
